title: HR Administration — Hiring, Paying, and Supporting the Federal Civilian Workforce
description: U.S. federal civilian human resources blueprint: one mission with the outcomes it seeks and ways to measure them, eleven capabilities from position management and onboarding through separation and workforce reporting, with their reference requirements, example implementation patterns with their tradeoffs, and discovery question sets for HR results and for HR operations. It follows Title 5 of the U.S. Code and OPM’s rules, including the 2025 Merit Hiring Plan and the move to one government-wide core HR system, and builds on Common Capabilities for case management, records, identity and access, and data protection.
jurisdictions: United States — federal executive agencies with civilian employees under Title 5

sources.title: OMB and OPM — Creating “Federal HR 2.0” by Consolidating Core Human Capital Management Across the Federal Government (December 10, 2025)
sources.note: Moves executive agencies onto one commercial core human capital management system, covering personnel action processing, the employee system of record, position management, self-service, analytics, time and attendance, and learning, connected to payroll, benefits, hiring, performance, and retirement systems. Agencies move in two waves from fiscal year 2026, with government-wide adoption the goal by fiscal year 2028, and pause their own core HR purchases and projects unless the OMB and OPM Directors grant an exception. The system will make eOPF and EHRI redundant. Military personnel and intelligence agencies aren’t included at first.

sources.title: White House Domestic Policy Council and OPM — Merit Hiring Plan (May 29, 2025)
sources.note: Carries out Executive Order 14170. Every competitive hiring process includes at least one technical or alternative assessment before the certificate, self-assessments are no longer used for ranking, and agencies use USAJOBS, USA Staffing, talent pools, and shared certificates. Sets the goal of time to initial offer under 80 days, and cites vetting goals of 21 days for low-risk positions, 25 days for non-sensitive moderate-risk positions, and 45 days for top secret, and 3 days when reciprocity applies.

sources.title: OPM — Reinvigorating Merit-Based Hiring Through Candidate Ranking in the Competitive and Excepted Service (Rule of Many), final rule (September 8, 2025)
sources.note: Lets agencies rank candidates by numerical score, with veterans’ preference points, and certify a set number of the highest-ranked to the hiring manager, using cut scores set by the assessment, business necessity, or a number or share of applicants. Effective November 7, 2025, with full compliance by March 9, 2026.

sources.title: OMB and OPM — Guidance on Executive Order 14356, Ensuring Continued Accountability in Federal Hiring (November 5, 2025)
sources.note: Each agency’s Strategic Hiring Committee approves the creation or filling of each vacancy, consistent with the Merit Hiring Plan and an Annual Staffing Plan the agency prepares with OMB and OPM, and gives OPM prompt written notice of approved hires.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 5107 — Classification of positions
sources.note: Each agency places each position under its jurisdiction in its appropriate class and grade in conformance with standards OPM publishes, and those actions are the basis for pay and personnel transactions.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 3327 — Civil service employment information
sources.note: Each agency promptly notifies OPM of each competitive service vacancy for which it seeks applications from people outside the federal service, and when applications will be accepted.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 3309 — Preference eligibles; examinations; additional points for
sources.note: A preference eligible who passes a competitive service examination receives 10 or 5 additional points above the earned rating, depending on the kind of preference.

sources.title: 5 CFR § 731.106 — Designation of public trust positions and investigative requirements
sources.note: The agency head designates each covered position at high, moderate, or low risk, which sets the investigation it needs, and people in public trust positions are subject to continuous vetting.

sources.title: 8 CFR § 274a.2 — Verification of identity and employment authorization
sources.note: The employee completes Section 1 of Form I-9 at the time of hire, and the employer examines the documents and completes Section 2 within three business days of the hire.

sources.title: 5 CFR § 930.301 — Information systems security awareness training program
sources.note: Agencies provide information security awareness material to all new employees before allowing them access to the systems, and all users of federal information systems see awareness material at least annually.

sources.title: 5 CFR § 2638.304 — Initial ethics training
sources.note: Each new employee subject to the Standards of Conduct completes initial ethics training within 3 months of appointment, covering financial conflicts of interest, impartiality, misuse of position, and gifts.

sources.title: 5 CFR § 724.203 — Training (No FEAR Act)
sources.note: Agencies train all employees on their rights and remedies under the antidiscrimination and whistleblower protection laws at least every 2 years, and, unless new employee orientation covers it, train new employees within 90 calendar days of appointment.

sources.title: Defense Civilian Personnel Advisory Service — DoD Onboarding Resource Portal (April 2, 2024)
sources.note: Guides, tip sheets, checklists, and templates for onboarding new, transferred, and promoted civilian employees, with the roles of supervisors, sponsors, and mentors, aimed at helping employees become productive quickly and stay.

sources.title: OPM — Guide to Processing Personnel Actions
sources.note: OPM’s instructions for personnel actions, revised continually (Update 112 took effect October 7, 2026). Most actions are approved by an appointing officer on or before their effective dates, and none takes effect before approval except as the guide allows. Agencies notify employees of every action, with an SF-50 for appointments, conversions, and separations, and report each action to EHRI accurately and on time.

sources.title: 5 CFR § 9.2 — Reporting workforce information
sources.note: The OPM Director may require executive agencies to report workforce information, sets the standards for it, and agencies make their submissions meet those standards consistent with the Privacy Act.

sources.title: OPM — Enterprise Human Resources Integration (EHRI)
sources.note: OPM’s government-wide HR data warehouse for about 2 million executive branch employees. Agencies send HR, payroll, and training data through standard interfaces, collected every two weeks, and retirement data to its standard. EHRI also hosts the electronic Official Personnel Folder.

sources.title: OPM — Federal Workforce Data
sources.note: OPM’s public site of federal civilian workforce data, updated monthly, covering employment, hiring, separations, pay, location, and demographics. It replaced FedScope in January 2026.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 5514 — Installment deduction for indebtedness to the United States
sources.note: Before collecting a debt from an employee’s pay, the agency gives at least 30 days’ written notice, a chance to inspect the records, to agree a repayment schedule, and to request a hearing. Deductions may not exceed 15 percent of disposable pay without the employee’s written consent.

sources.title: 5 CFR § 890.301 — Opportunities for employees to enroll or change enrollment (Federal Employees Health Benefits)
sources.note: An employee who becomes eligible may elect to enroll or not to enroll within 60 days after becoming eligible.

sources.title: OPM — Online Retirement Application (ORA)
sources.note: OPM’s fully digital system that replaces the paper retirement process. The employee’s HR office starts the application, which is prefilled from EHRI and eOPF data, and the applicant, HR, and payroll share one view of its status.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 4302 — Establishment of performance appraisal systems
sources.note: Each performance appraisal system communicates performance standards and critical elements to each employee at the beginning of each appraisal period, evaluates employees against them, assists employees in improving unacceptable performance, and reassigns, reduces in grade, or removes those who continue to perform unacceptably only after an opportunity to demonstrate acceptable performance.

sources.title: 5 CFR Part 430, Subpart B — Performance Appraisal for General Schedule, Prevailing Rate, and Certain Other Employees
sources.note: Performance plans are provided at the beginning of each appraisal period, normally within 30 days, and the appraisal period is generally 12 months (§ 430.206). Programs use one of OPM’s rating patterns, and OPM may set a standardized distribution of rating levels (§ 430.208). Amended by a final rule effective August 6, 2026, with compliance with the new rating patterns and distribution by January 1, 2027.

sources.title: OPM — FY 2026 Standardized Distribution of Rating Levels and FY 2026 Performance Awards Guidance for Federal Employees (September 21, 2026)
sources.note: Caps Level 4 and Level 5 ratings at 40 percent of each covered population, career SES, Senior Professional, and General Schedule employees, for appraisal periods ending September 30, 2026, as a ceiling, not a target. At least 60 percent of each bonus pool should go to Level 4 and Level 5 performers.

sources.title: 5 CFR § 11.5 — Civil Service Rule XI, finalizing probationary appointments
sources.note: Added by Executive Order 14284 of April 24, 2025, and amended August 3, 2026. Within the last 30 days of a probationary or trial period, the agency head or a designated official certifies in writing whether the employee’s continued employment will advance the public interest; without certification, the employee’s service ends with the period.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 7513 — Cause and procedure (adverse actions)
sources.note: An employee against whom an adverse action is proposed is entitled to at least 30 days’ advance written notice with the specific reasons, unless there is reasonable cause to believe the employee committed a crime punishable by imprisonment, at least 7 days to answer orally and in writing, representation, and a written decision with its specific reasons.

sources.title: 5 CFR § 351.801 — Notice period (reduction in force)
sources.note: Each competing employee selected for release is entitled to specific written notice at least 60 full days before the effective date, or at least 30 full days when OPM approves a shorter period for circumstances not reasonably foreseeable.

sources.title: OPM — Reduction in Force, final rule, 91 FR 49178 (August 3, 2026)
sources.note: Rewrites subparts B through H of 5 CFR Part 351 for notices issued on or after September 2, 2026. Employees are ranked by tenure group, then by performance credit with veterans’ preference, with tenure subgroup and service computation date as tie-breakers, and each notice lists the factors used.

sources.title: 5 CFR § 293.302 — Establishment of the Official Personnel Folder
sources.note: Each agency establishes an Official Personnel Folder for each employee, and except as OPM’s Guide to Personnel Recordkeeping provides, only one is kept for each employee.

sources.title: National Archives — General Records Schedule 2.2, Employee Management Records
sources.note: Covers records of supervising employees, processing personnel actions, and managing performance, including the Official Personnel Folder and its electronic equivalent, with how long each is kept and when separated employees’ folders are transferred (Transmittal 35, May 2024).

sources.title: OMB Memorandum M-25-21 — Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust (April 3, 2025)
sources.note: AI whose output is a principal basis for decisions with a significant effect on rights or safety is high-impact, and AI used to determine the terms or conditions of federal employment, including pre-employment screening, pay or promotion, performance management, hiring or termination, or recommending disciplinary action, is presumed to be (§ 6(n)). High-impact uses need testing, an impact assessment, monitoring, human oversight, and human review and appeal (§ 4(b)).

sources.title: NIST — Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.note: A framework for voluntary use in managing the risks of AI systems, built around four functions, govern, map, measure, and manage, and the characteristics of trustworthy AI, such as being valid, accountable, and fair.

elements.title: HR Administration
elements.description: Hire, pay, and support the agency’s civilian employees under the merit system: fill the positions the agency needs on merit and on time, give new employees a good start, process each personnel action correctly, pay people accurately, manage their performance, handle conduct fairly, see them through retirement or separation, and keep the records and data the law requires.

attributes.tagline: Hiring, paying, and supporting the federal civilian workforce
principles: Each employee has one record, from the job offer to retirement, in one system of record
Personnel actions are entered once and reach payroll, benefits, retirement, and OPM without retyping
Positions are records of their own, with their classification, funding, and approvals
Each new employee follows one onboarding journey, from the offer through their first year, with everything ready on day one
Hiring uses validated assessments and ranks candidates by score, with veterans’ preference, and tells applicants where they stand
Managers and employees do routine tasks themselves, such as updating details or starting a request
Workforce figures come from the system of record, not from spreadsheets
AI drafts documents and answers policy questions, and people make every decision about a person’s employment

elements.title: The agency fills the positions it needs on time
elements.description: Approved positions are announced, assessed, and offered quickly enough that the work doesn’t wait, within the government-wide goal of under 80 days to an initial offer.

measures.title: Time to initial offer
measures.description: The days from the start of a hiring action to the initial job offer, by office and kind of position, against the government-wide goal of under 80 days. OPM tracks it on its hiring compliance dashboard.

elements.title: People are hired on merit, with veterans’ preference
elements.description: Vacancies are open to the people the law allows to apply, candidates are ranked on validated assessments of their skills, and veterans’ preference is applied as the law requires.

measures.title: Hiring actions with a technical or alternative assessment
measures.description: The share of competitive hiring actions that used at least one technical or alternative assessment before the certificate was issued, rather than a self-assessment alone.

measures.title: Certificates returned without a selection
measures.description: The share of certificates of eligible candidates that hiring managers returned without selecting anyone, which can mean the assessment didn’t find the right people.

elements.title: New employees start well, vetted, equipped, and supported
elements.description: Each new employee is vetted promptly to the level their position needs, finds their equipment, accounts, and credential ready on their first day, and has an orientation, a sponsor, and their supervisor’s attention through their first year, so they become effective quickly and stay.

measures.title: Vetting completed within the timeliness goals
measures.description: The share of new employees whose vetting finished within the goals the Merit Hiring Plan cites, 21 days for low-risk positions, 25 days for non-sensitive moderate-risk positions, and 45 days for top secret, and within 3 days when reciprocity applies.

measures.title: New employees ready to work on their first day
measures.description: The share of new employees whose equipment, accounts, credential, and workspace were ready on their first day, from the onboarding tasks or a short question to each new employee.

measures.title: New employee training completed on time
measures.description: The share of new employees who completed security awareness training before their system access, initial ethics training within 3 months, and No FEAR Act training within 90 days.

measures.title: New employees who leave in their first year
measures.description: The share of new employees who separate within a year of starting, by office and occupation, from the separations the agency reports to OPM.

elements.title: Personnel actions are correct and take effect on time
elements.description: Each appointment, promotion, change, and separation is approved by its effective date, coded correctly, and reported to OPM accurately, so pay, benefits, and records follow without correction.

measures.title: Actions processed after their effective date
measures.description: The share of personnel actions processed after the date they took effect, by kind of action and office.

measures.title: Errors returned from OPM’s data screening
measures.description: The number of errors OPM finds when it screens each submission to its Enterprise Human Resources Integration data warehouse, and how long they take to fix.

elements.title: Employees are paid correctly and on time
elements.description: Pay, leave, and deductions follow each employee’s personnel actions and approved time, so overpayments and the debts they create are rare.

measures.title: Pay debts established
measures.description: The number and amount of debts established because an employee was overpaid, by cause, such as a late personnel action or a time and attendance error.

elements.title: Retiring employees get their annuity without delay
elements.description: The agency prepares each retirement application completely and sends it to OPM promptly, so OPM can begin paying the annuity without returning it for more information.

measures.title: Days from retirement to submission to OPM
measures.description: The days from each employee’s retirement date to the agency’s submission of the complete application to OPM, through HR and payroll.

elements.title: Employees know what’s expected and are rated on it
elements.description: Each employee has a performance plan at the start of the appraisal period, is rated against it at the end, and ratings distinguish levels of performance as OPM’s rules require.

measures.title: Performance plans and ratings on time
measures.description: The share of employees given a performance plan within 30 days of the appraisal period’s start, and the share with a rating of record soon after it ends.

measures.title: Share of ratings at the top two levels
measures.description: The share of employees in each covered population rated at Level 4 or Level 5, against OPM’s cap, which is 40 percent for the 2026 appraisal cycle.

elements.title: Discipline and removals are fair and hold up on appeal
elements.description: Each adverse or performance-based action gives the employee the notice, time to reply, and decision the law requires, rests on a documented record, and stands up when appealed.

measures.title: Actions sustained on appeal
measures.description: The number of adverse and performance-based actions appealed, and the share that were sustained, settled, or reversed.

elements.title: The workforce’s data is open to view
elements.description: The agency reports complete, accurate workforce data to OPM on schedule, so the public can see the size, hiring, pay, and separations of the federal workforce each month.

measures.title: Workforce data submitted on schedule
measures.description: The share of the agency’s scheduled submissions to EHRI accepted on time, which feed OPM’s monthly Federal Workforce Data site.

elements.title: Workforce & Position Management
elements.description: Ability to plan the staff the agency needs each year, keep each position as a record with its organization, classification, and funding, classify positions against OPM’s standards, and get the approvals each new or vacant position needs before it’s filled.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Since October 2025, each agency’s Strategic Hiring Committee approves the creation or filling of every vacancy against the agency’s Annual Staffing Plan. Many agencies keep position data in a separate tool today; the government-wide core HR system includes position management.

elements.title: Recruitment & Hiring
elements.description: Ability to announce vacancies on USAJOBS, assess applicants with validated, skills-based assessments, rank them by score with veterans’ preference, issue certificates to hiring managers, and make offers, sharing certificates and talent pools across offices and agencies.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Excepted service and special hiring authorities, such as for veterans or people with disabilities, follow their own rules. Agencies had to comply with the Rule of Many by March 9, 2026.

elements.title: Pre-Employment & Vetting
elements.description: Ability to designate each position’s risk and sensitivity, and between the tentative offer and the first day, start each selectee’s background investigation and credential, verify their eligibility to work, and set a start date the vetting allows.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Agencies with delegated investigative authority run some of their own background investigations. Reciprocity lets a previously vetted person start sooner, and the Merit Hiring Plan asks for vetting within 3 days when it applies.

elements.title: New Employee Onboarding
elements.description: Ability to give each new employee a good start, with their equipment, accounts, credential, and workspace ready on their first day, an orientation, a sponsor who helps them settle in, the training every new employee needs assigned and tracked, and check-ins with their supervisor through their first year.
elements.applicabilityNotes: The same steps suit employees who transfer in or are promoted into a new role. Day-one readiness depends on IT, facilities, and security teams outside HR, and employees who work remotely need their equipment and accounts working before they start.

elements.title: Personnel Action Processing
elements.description: Ability to request, approve, and process each personnel action, such as an appointment, promotion, reassignment, or change in pay, coded as OPM’s guide directs, approved by its effective date, and sent to payroll and the employee’s record.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Most agencies process actions through an HR shared service provider or a department system today, and will move to the government-wide core HR system in their wave.

elements.title: Pay & Leave Administration
elements.description: Ability to record and approve each employee’s time and leave, pay them correctly each pay period from their personnel actions, and, when someone is overpaid, give the notice and choices the law requires before collecting.
elements.applicabilityNotes: A federal payroll provider calculates and pays salaries for most agencies. The agency owns the personnel actions and approved time that payroll runs on.

elements.title: Benefits & Retirement
elements.description: Ability to offer new employees their benefits, such as health and life insurance and the Thrift Savings Plan, within their enrollment periods, counsel employees nearing retirement, and prepare and certify each retirement application to OPM.
elements.applicabilityNotes: OPM decides retirement eligibility and pays annuities; the agency prepares the application, certifies the service history, and sends it on through payroll.

elements.title: Performance Management
elements.description: Ability to give each employee a performance plan at the start of the appraisal period, check in during it, rate them against it at the end within OPM’s rating distribution, and certify each probationer’s continued employment before the probationary period ends.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Agencies must move to OPM’s new rating patterns and apply its distribution caps by January 1, 2027. Senior Executive Service ratings follow their own rules.

elements.title: Employee Relations & Conduct
elements.description: Ability to help managers address misconduct and poor performance, give employees an opportunity to improve where the law requires one, propose and decide adverse actions with the notice and reply the law requires, and keep the record that supports each action if it’s appealed.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Agency counsel often advises on proposed actions. Collective bargaining agreements can add steps for employees in a bargaining unit.

elements.title: Separations & Workforce Reshaping
elements.description: Ability to process each resignation, retirement, removal, and reduction in force with the right notices, final pay, and clearance, and, in a reduction in force, rank employees by the retention factors in OPM’s rules.
elements.applicabilityNotes: OPM rewrote its reduction in force rules for notices issued on or after September 2, 2026, ranking employees by performance credit with veterans’ preference within each tenure group, with length of service as the tie-breaker.

elements.title: Personnel Records & Workforce Reporting
elements.description: Ability to keep one Official Personnel Folder for each employee, move it with them between agencies and to the National Archives when they leave, and report the agency’s workforce data to OPM accurately and on schedule.
elements.applicabilityNotes: OPM runs the electronic Official Personnel Folder and EHRI for most agencies. The government-wide core HR system is meant to replace both once agencies have moved to it.

elements.title: Get each new or vacant position approved before filling it
elements.description: Have the agency’s Strategic Hiring Committee approve the creation or filling of each vacancy, consistent with the Annual Staffing Plan prepared with OMB and OPM at the start of each fiscal year, and notify OPM promptly in writing of approved hires.

elements.title: Classify each position against OPM’s standards
elements.description: Place each position in its class and grade in conformance with the standards OPM publishes, and record the classification that pay and personnel actions rest on.

elements.title: Announce vacancies open to applicants from outside the government
elements.description: Notify OPM promptly of each competitive service vacancy for which the agency seeks applications from outside the federal service, and say when applications will be accepted.

elements.title: Use at least one technical or alternative assessment before the certificate
elements.description: Include at least one technical or alternative assessment in every competitive hiring process before the certificate is issued, tell applicants how they’ll be assessed, and use self-assessments only for minimum qualifications and eligibility.

elements.title: Rank candidates by score, with veterans’ preference
elements.description: Add 5 or 10 points to the passing scores of preference eligibles as the law provides, rank candidates in score order, and certify the number the agency’s Rule of Many method sets.

elements.title: Designate each position’s risk level
elements.description: Designate each covered position at high, moderate, or low risk, so each person is investigated to the level the position needs, and enroll employees in continuous vetting.

elements.title: Verify each new employee’s eligibility to work within 3 business days
elements.description: Have each new employee complete Section 1 of Form I-9 at the time of hire, and examine their documents and complete Section 2 within three business days of the hire.

elements.title: Complete vetting within the government’s timeliness goals
elements.description: Aim to finish vetting within 21 days for low-risk positions, 25 days for non-sensitive moderate-risk positions, and 45 days for top secret, and within 3 days when reciprocity applies, using preliminary determinations where allowed.

elements.title: Give security awareness training before system access
elements.description: Give each new employee information security awareness training before allowing them access to the agency’s systems, and refresh it at least once a year.

elements.title: Complete initial ethics training within 3 months
elements.description: Have each new employee subject to the Standards of Conduct complete initial ethics training, on conflicts of interest, impartiality, misuse of position, and gifts, within 3 months of appointment.

elements.title: Train new employees on the No FEAR Act within 90 days
elements.description: Train each new employee on their rights and remedies under the antidiscrimination and whistleblower protection laws within 90 calendar days of appointment, unless new employee orientation covers it, and all employees at least every 2 years.

elements.title: Approve each personnel action by its effective date
elements.description: Have an appointing officer approve most personnel actions on or before their effective dates, since no action can take effect before it’s approved except as OPM’s guide allows, and code each one as the guide directs.

elements.title: Tell each employee about every personnel action taken on them
elements.description: Give employees an SF-50 for appointments, conversions, and separations, and an electronic or paper notice they can print for other actions, without making them ask whether an action was processed.

elements.title: Give notice and choices before collecting an overpayment from pay
elements.description: Give at least 30 days’ written notice of the debt and the plan to collect it from pay, a chance to inspect the records, to agree a repayment schedule, and to request a hearing, and deduct no more than 15 percent of disposable pay without consent.

elements.title: Let new employees enroll in health benefits within 60 days
elements.description: Give each newly eligible employee the information and chance to enroll in the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, or not, within 60 days after they become eligible.

elements.title: Prepare and certify retirement applications in OPM’s online system
elements.description: Start each retirement application in OPM’s Online Retirement Application, review the employee’s documents, certify the summary of service, and send the package through payroll to OPM.

elements.title: Give each employee a performance plan at the start of the appraisal period
elements.description: Communicate each employee’s critical elements and performance standards at the beginning of the appraisal period, normally within 30 days, and rate them against those standards at its end.

elements.title: Keep ratings within OPM’s distribution of rating levels
elements.description: Use one of OPM’s rating patterns, and keep the share of each covered population rated at the top levels within the cap OPM sets each year, which for 2026 is 40 percent at Levels 4 and 5 combined.

elements.title: Certify each probationer before the probationary period ends
elements.description: Have the agency head or a designated official decide in writing, within the last 30 days of each probationary or trial period, whether the employee’s continued employment will advance the public interest; without that certification, the employee’s service ends with the period.

elements.title: Give 30 days’ notice and 7 days to reply before an adverse action
elements.description: Give the employee at least 30 days’ written notice with the specific reasons, at least 7 days to answer orally and in writing, the right to a representative, and a written decision with its reasons, except where the law allows a shorter notice.

elements.title: Give an opportunity to improve before acting on poor performance
elements.description: Help an employee whose performance is unacceptable to improve, and reassign, reduce in grade, or remove them for it only after an opportunity to demonstrate acceptable performance.

elements.title: Give at least 60 days’ notice before release in a reduction in force
elements.description: Give each employee released in a reduction in force specific written notice at least 60 full days before the release, or at least 30 days with OPM’s approval when the cause wasn’t foreseeable, with the retention factors the ranking used.

elements.title: Keep one Official Personnel Folder for each employee
elements.description: Keep a single Official Personnel Folder, or its approved electronic equivalent, for each employee, with the records OPM’s rules require, and keep or transfer it as General Records Schedule 2.2 directs when the employee leaves.

elements.title: Report workforce data to OPM accurately and on schedule
elements.description: Send OPM the personnel action, status, payroll, and other workforce data it requires, in its data standards and on its schedule, and fix the errors its screening returns.

elements.title: One Core HR System of Record
elements.description: An example architecture: one core human capital management system holds each employee’s record, each position, and each personnel action, gives managers and employees self-service, records time and attendance, and sends actions to payroll, benefits, retirement, and OPM.

parts: The employee record, from the job offer to separation, with each personnel action on it
Positions as records of their own, with their organization, classification, funding, and approvals
Requests for personnel actions from managers, routed for approval by the appointing officer before the effective date
Self-service for employees and managers, such as changes of address, benefits, and direct deposit
Time and attendance, approved by supervisors each pay period
Connections to hiring, payroll, benefits, retirement, performance, and learning systems
Reports and dashboards from the same records
strengths: One record for each employee and position, instead of copies in several systems
Actions entered once reach payroll and OPM without retyping
Workforce figures come from the system of record
fitsWhen: Every executive agency with civilian employees, since OMB and OPM are moving all of them to one system
watchFor: Moving decades of records needs early work on which data moves, which is kept elsewhere, and which is cleaned first
Each agency-unique practice either fits the common system or has to be given up, so they need listing and deciding early
Connections to payroll and other systems often take the most work

elements.title: Hiring through USAJOBS and USA Staffing with Validated Assessments
elements.description: An example architecture: vacancies are posted on USAJOBS, applicants are assessed with validated, skills-based assessments, ranked by score with veterans’ preference, and certified to hiring managers in OPM’s USA Staffing, with talent pools and shared certificates reaching across offices and agencies.

parts: Job announcements on USAJOBS that say how applicants will be assessed
A short eligibility questionnaire, then technical assessments such as USA Hire, structured interviews, or work samples
Scores with veterans’ preference points, ranked and certified by the agency’s Rule of Many method
Talent pools and shared certificates, so one assessment can fill several positions
Automatic notices to applicants at each stage
Hiring data that shows time to hire and assessment use
strengths: Applicants find and apply for every job in one place
Validated assessments rank on skills instead of how applicants rate themselves
Shared certificates and talent pools cut the time to the next hire
fitsWhen: The agency still ranks applicants with self-assessments
Several offices hire for the same kinds of positions
watchFor: Validated assessments exist for many job series but not all, so some need subject matter experts to build them
OPM plans to merge USAJOBS and USA Staffing, so steps and connections may change

elements.title: Pre-Employment Steps Connected to Vetting, E-Verify, and Credentials
elements.description: An example architecture: each tentative offer starts one pre-employment case that sends the selectee’s forms to the background investigation system, checks employment eligibility through E-Verify, orders the identity credential, and tracks each step to the first day.

parts: A pre-employment case for each selectee, opened from the tentative offer
Investigation forms sent to the background investigation system, with the position’s risk designation
Form I-9 completed online, with E-Verify checks
Identity credential and system accounts ordered once vetting allows
Status for the selectee, the hiring manager, and HR at each step
strengths: Selectees fill in each form once
Everyone can see what’s holding up a start date
Vetting starts the day the offer is made
fitsWhen: Onboarding runs on email, PDFs, and spreadsheets
Start dates often slip while vetting and credentials catch up
watchFor: Each connection to a vetting or credential system needs approval and keeping up
Preliminary determinations and reciprocity rules need to be set up correctly to save time

elements.title: A Guided Onboarding Journey for New Employees
elements.description: An example architecture: each new employee follows one onboarding journey, from the tentative offer through their first year, that shows them what comes next, sends tasks to IT, facilities, security, the supervisor, and a sponsor so everything is ready on day one, assigns the training every new employee needs, and prompts check-ins along the way.

parts: A personal onboarding page for each new employee, with each step, its owner, and its date
Forms completed online before the first day, prefilled where the agency already has the information
Tasks for IT, facilities, security, and the supervisor, with deadlines before the first day, for equipment, accounts, credential, and workspace
A sponsor named for each new employee, with a short guide to the role
An orientation schedule, and the training every new employee needs assigned with its due date, security awareness before system access first
Check-ins with the supervisor at set points, such as 30, 60, and 90 days, starting with the performance plan
A short survey after the first few months, with results by office
strengths: New employees know what comes next instead of waiting to be told
Day-one readiness is tracked as tasks with owners, not hoped for
Required training doesn’t slip past its deadlines
Supervisors and sponsors get prompts at the moments that matter
fitsWhen: Onboarding steps live in email, checklists, and people’s memories
New employees often start without equipment or accounts
Many new employees work remotely or at sites away from HR
watchFor: Tasks for teams outside HR only work if those teams accept them, with owners and deadlines
A portal doesn’t replace a supervisor and sponsor who make time for the new employee
Too many steps on day one overwhelm people, so spread them over the first weeks

elements.title: Payroll from a Federal Payroll Provider
elements.description: An example architecture: a federal payroll provider calculates each employee’s pay every pay period from the agency’s personnel actions and approved time, pays salaries, withholds taxes and benefits, and manages pay debts with the notices the law requires.

parts: Personnel actions and approved time received from the core HR system each pay period
Pay, deductions, and leave balances calculated and paid
Earnings and leave statements for employees
Overpayments found, with debt notices, repayment agreements, and hearing requests handled
Payroll data sent to OPM and to the agency’s financial system
strengths: Payroll rules and tax changes are kept up by the provider for many agencies
The agency doesn’t run its own payroll system
fitsWhen: Most executive agencies, which pay employees through one of a few federal payroll providers
watchFor: Late or wrong personnel actions are the most common cause of pay errors, so the hand-off from HR needs watching
Changes to the core HR system need testing with the payroll provider before they go live

elements.title: Retirement Applications through OPM’s Online Retirement Application
elements.description: An example architecture: HR starts each retirement application in OPM’s Online Retirement Application, prefilled from EHRI and eOPF data, the employee completes it online, HR reviews and certifies the summary of service, and payroll certifies its part before the package goes to OPM.

parts: Applications started by HR with the employee’s email, prefilled with service history, salary, and sick leave from EHRI and eOPF
Documents uploaded by the employee and reviewed by HR
A summary of service certified by HR
Payroll’s certification, then submission to OPM
One view of each application’s status for the employee, HR, and payroll
strengths: Replaces the paper process, so applications reach OPM sooner and complete
Prefilled data cuts errors in service and salary history
Everyone sees the same status
fitsWhen: Every agency whose employees retire under the federal retirement systems
watchFor: Prefilled data is only as good as the agency’s records, so gaps in service history still need finding early
HR specialists and payroll staff need access and training before a wave of retirements

elements.title: Electronic Personnel Folders and Workforce Data through OPM
elements.description: An example architecture: each employee’s Official Personnel Folder is kept electronically in OPM’s eOPF, and the agency’s personnel action, status, and payroll data reach OPM’s Enterprise Human Resources Integration warehouse on schedule, screened and corrected, for OPM’s reports and public data.

parts: An electronic personnel folder for each employee, with documents filed as OPM’s recordkeeping guide directs
Folders that move with employees between agencies, and to the National Personnel Records Center when they leave
Regular submissions of personnel action, status, and payroll data to EHRI in OPM’s data standards
Error lists returned by OPM, worked and corrected at the source
Data that feeds OPM’s retirement processing and its public Federal Workforce Data site
strengths: One folder for each employee across their federal career
The agency’s data reaches OPM’s reports and the public without a separate effort
fitsWhen: Every agency, until the government-wide core HR system replaces these systems
watchFor: Errors fixed in EHRI but not in the agency’s own system come back next time
OMB and OPM plan to retire eOPF and EHRI once the core HR system is in place, so new connections to them should be few

elements.title: Performance Plans and Appraisals Online
elements.description: An example architecture: performance plans, check-ins, and ratings are kept online, plans go to employees at the start of the appraisal period, ratings are checked against OPM’s distribution cap before they’re final, and ratings of record reach the core HR system and personnel folder.

parts: Performance plans with critical elements and standards, built from templates for each kind of position
Acknowledgment by each employee at the start of the period, and check-ins during it
Ratings proposed by supervisors and reviewed by higher-level officials
A view of proposed ratings against OPM’s cap, by covered population, before ratings are final
Ratings of record sent to the core HR system, the personnel folder, and awards
Probationers’ end dates, with reminders for each certification decision
strengths: Plans and ratings are on time and in one place
Leaders can see the distribution before ratings are final, not after
Ratings flow to awards and to reduction in force retention without retyping
fitsWhen: Plans and ratings are kept on paper or in documents
The agency needs to change rating patterns and apply the cap by January 2027
watchFor: Templates help consistency but can make standards too general to rate against
Probationary certifications have a hard deadline, so reminders need an owner

elements.title: AI Help Drafting HR Documents and Answering Policy Questions
elements.description: An example architecture: HR specialists and managers use an AI model, in an environment the agency approves, to draft position descriptions, job analyses, announcements, and interview questions from OPM’s standards and the agency’s templates, and to find answers in OPM’s guides, and then check and finish each draft themselves. It isn’t used to screen, rate, or rank applicants or employees.

parts: An AI model in an environment the agency has approved for HR information
OPM’s classification and qualification standards, its processing and recordkeeping guides, and the agency’s templates as reference material
Drafts shown with the sources they drew on
HR specialists and managers who check, correct, and approve each draft
Rules that keep the model away from decisions about people, such as screening applicants or proposing ratings
strengths: Specialists start from a draft instead of a blank page
Answers point to the guide and section they came from
Managers can get help writing clear job requirements before they reach HR
fitsWhen: Writing position descriptions and announcements takes much of the time to hire
HR specialists field many routine policy questions
watchFor: Drafts can be wrong or cite rules that have changed, as many did in 2025 and 2026, so specialists check each one
Using AI to decide the terms of someone’s employment, such as hiring, pay, ratings, or discipline, is presumed high-impact under OMB’s AI memo
The agency’s AI governance may require a listing in its AI use case inventory first

elements.title: Workforce Analytics from Core HR Data
elements.description: An example architecture: an analytics workspace draws on the core HR, hiring, payroll, and performance data to show hiring against the staffing plan, time to hire, retirement eligibility and attrition, ratings against the cap, and data errors before they reach OPM.

parts: Regular feeds from the core HR system, hiring, payroll, and performance tools
Hiring against the Annual Staffing Plan, by office and occupation
Time to hire by step, so delays show where they happen
Retirement eligibility and departures, by office and skill
Plans, ratings, and probationary certifications due or overdue
Checks of the agency’s data against OPM’s standards before each submission
strengths: Leaders see gaps coming before positions sit empty
The same figures support the staffing plan, OPM’s reports, and the agency’s own decisions
fitsWhen: Reports are built by hand from several systems
Leaders ask the same workforce questions every month
watchFor: Person-level HR data is sensitive, so who sees what needs setting with care
Figures defined differently from OPM’s, such as time to hire, need reconciling first

elements.title: Merit Hiring Plan resources
elements.description: Guidance, FAQs, and fact sheets for putting the Merit Hiring Plan in place, on applications, assessments, pooled hiring, and Rule of Many ranking, with a webinar series and templates such as a sample Rule of Many policy.

elements.title: Assessment and selection
elements.description: How to assess applicants, from job analysis and competencies to structured interviews and other assessment methods, and how to design an assessment strategy for a position.

elements.title: Classification and qualifications
elements.description: OPM’s grading criteria for the General Schedule and Federal Wage System, draft standards, classification flysheets, and the government-wide qualification standards, for anyone classifying positions or writing job requirements.

elements.title: DoD Onboarding Resource Portal
elements.description: A 2024 collection of guides, tip sheets, checklists, and templates for onboarding new, transferred, and promoted civilian employees, with what supervisors, sponsors, and mentors each do, useful well beyond Defense.

attributes.by: Defense Civilian Personnel Advisory Service, Department of Defense

elements.title: Guide to Processing Personnel Actions
elements.description: OPM’s instructions for preparing personnel actions and keeping the Official Personnel Folder, revised as rules change, alongside the Guide to Personnel Recordkeeping.

elements.title: Online Retirement Application — Human Resources Specialist Guide
elements.description: A 2025 step-by-step guide for HR specialists using OPM’s Online Retirement Application, from creating the applicant’s profile through the pre-application and the certified summary of service to sending the package to payroll.

elements.title: Performance management
elements.description: OPM’s Performance Management Playbook for agency leaders, toolkits for managers and employees, and the memos and rules on rating patterns and distribution, including the 2026 changes.

elements.title: Employee relations
elements.description: The laws, rules, and precedents for addressing conduct and performance, including adverse and performance-based actions, appeals, and alternative dispute resolution, with training and an interagency network of employee relations managers.

elements.title: Reductions in force
elements.description: A summary of the reduction in force rules, the notice employees must receive, a guide to pay, leave, and benefits for employees, and handbooks for agencies.

elements.title: Federal Workforce Data
elements.description: OPM’s open data site on the federal civilian workforce, updated monthly, with employment, hiring, separations, pay, location, and demographics to explore and download. It replaced FedScope in January 2026.

elements.title: OPM’s government-wide core HR system
elements.description: The single commercial core HR platform OMB and OPM are moving executive agencies onto under Federal HR 2.0, in two waves from fiscal year 2026, with government-wide adoption the goal by 2028.

strengths: One system across government, so employees moving between agencies keep one record
It will make the separate eOPF and EHRI systems unnecessary over time
fitsWhen: The agency’s wave has begun, or it’s preparing data, connections, and staff for it
watchFor: Agencies were told to pause their own core HR purchases and projects, with exceptions only from the OMB and OPM Directors
Military personnel and intelligence agencies aren’t included at first

elements.title: The agency’s current HR shared service provider
elements.description: The core HR system the agency uses today through a federal HR shared service provider or its department, until its move to the government-wide system.

strengths: Already in place, with staff who know it
fitsWhen: The agency’s wave hasn’t begun yet
watchFor: Changes worth making now are the ones that also prepare for the move, such as cleaning data and documenting connections

elements.title: OPM’s USA Staffing
elements.description: OPM’s talent acquisition system, used with USAJOBS and USA Hire, which the Merit Hiring Plan asks agencies to use.

strengths: Built for federal hiring rules and OPM’s hiring data
Shared certificates and talent pools work across agencies that use it
fitsWhen: Most agencies, especially those changing how they assess applicants
watchFor: Each agency still sets up its own assessments, ranking method, and approvals

elements.title: A talent acquisition product connected to USAJOBS
elements.description: A commercial talent acquisition product that posts to USAJOBS and sends hiring data to OPM.

strengths: Can suit agencies with unusual hiring authorities or very high volume
fitsWhen: The agency already runs one and it meets the Merit Hiring Plan’s steps
watchFor: Shared certificates and OPM’s hiring data are harder outside USA Staffing

elements.title: The talent acquisition system’s onboarding
elements.description: The onboarding features of the agency’s talent acquisition system, connected to the vetting, E-Verify, and credentialing systems.

strengths: Picks up where the hiring action ends, with no retyping
fitsWhen: The agency uses USA Staffing or a product with onboarding
watchFor: Connections the Merit Hiring Plan names, such as to background investigations and credentials, may still need building

elements.title: The core HR system’s onboarding and learning
elements.description: The new employee self-service, onboarding, and learning features of the agency’s core HR system, which the government-wide system includes.

strengths: The employee record, training, and onboarding steps share one system
fitsWhen: The agency’s core HR system offers onboarding journeys
watchFor: Tasks for IT, facilities, and security may still need sending to the systems those teams use

elements.title: The agency’s shared service or case platform
elements.description: Onboarding journeys built on the platform the agency already uses for IT and facilities requests, with tasks routed to each team.

strengths: Tasks land in the queues IT, facilities, and security already work from
fitsWhen: Day-one readiness is the biggest problem, and those teams already use the platform
watchFor: Training assignments and the employee record stay in the HR systems, so connections are needed

elements.title: An onboarding product
elements.description: An onboarding product connected to the core HR system and the agency’s request systems.

strengths: Built for a new employee’s experience, with welcome content and check-ins
fitsWhen: The agency hires many people a year across many sites
watchFor: Another product to buy and keep up, and its data and connections may need moving when the agency joins the government-wide core HR system

elements.title: The agency’s federal payroll provider
elements.description: The federal payroll provider that serves the agency, fed with its personnel actions and approved time.

elements.title: OPM’s Online Retirement Application
elements.description: OPM’s Online Retirement Application, prefilled from EHRI and eOPF and completed by the employee, HR, and payroll.

elements.title: OPM’s eOPF and EHRI
elements.description: OPM’s eOPF for personnel folders and EHRI for workforce data, with the agency’s data sent on schedule.

elements.title: The HR provider’s performance tool
elements.description: The performance management tool the agency’s HR shared service provider or department offers, connected to its core HR system.

strengths: Shares data with the core HR system the agency already uses
fitsWhen: The provider’s tool supports OPM’s current rating patterns
watchFor: The connection to the government-wide core HR system will need building when the agency moves

elements.title: A performance management product
elements.description: A performance management product configured for OPM’s rules and connected to the core HR system.

strengths: Can offer better check-ins and goal setting than a basic tool
fitsWhen: The agency’s current tool can’t meet the new rules
watchFor: Another product to buy and keep up, and to connect to the core HR system

elements.title: An AI model the agency approves
elements.description: An AI model in an environment the agency has approved, used with OPM’s standards and the agency’s templates to draft HR documents.

elements.title: An analytics workspace
elements.description: HR data brought together in the agency’s analytics tools.

strengths: Joins data from every HR system the agency uses
fitsWhen: The agency has analytics tools and people who use them
watchFor: Feeds need rebuilding when the agency moves to the government-wide core HR system
